newsitem.title: USA: U.S. holds fire against South African criticism.
newsitem.headline: U.S. holds fire against South African criticism.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday held its fire in the face of criticism from South African President Nelson Mandela and said its warning against arms sales to Syria applied to any prospective seller, not just Pretoria.
"We've pretty much said what we want to say about this matter," State Department deputy spokesman Glyn Davies told reporters when asked about Mandela's comments in Johannesburg.

"The essence of it is that the United States would urge any government that may be interested in the sale of arms to countries on the terrorism list not to sell arms to countries on the terrorism list," Davies said.
"I'm not going to get into reacting to their further reaction," he added.
Mandela, angrily rejecting U.S. warnings over a proposed arms deal with Syria, said earlier that South Africa would deal with anyone it wanted to, regardless of outside pressure.

"We will conclude agreements with any country whether they are popular in the West or not. And that is what we are likely to do in this case," he told reporters at his home, one week before his cabinet is due to take a final decision. "The enemies of countries in the West are not our enemies."

The South African Foreign Ministry has said any deal with Syria for what it termed "software" was not likely to be concluded before 1999 and that three European countries were also bidding for the business. It declined to name them.

The dispute began after Washington said on Monday it was extremely concerned that Pretoria planned to sell $641 million of aim-enhancing gear for Soviet-made tanks to Syria, which is on the U.S. list of states that allegedly back terrorism along with North Korea, Iran, Iraq, Libya, Sudan and Cuba.
Washington threatened to cut off aid worth $110 million this year if the deal went ahead. But, in a tough statement that may sour ties further, Mandela said such pressure would not work.

"We will never allow any support or assistance from any country, no matter how powerful it is, to dictate our foreign policy, nor allow any country to violate our sovereignty and undermine our national pride," he said.

Mandela, 78, has often brushed aside more muted criticism of his friendship with other U.S. bogeymen such as Libya, Iran and Cuba, despite appeals from political commentators not to alienate the world's most powerful nation. Washington's latest public criticism seems to have enraged him.
